AB.key_differentiator: Plan A delivers a clean, matched event-study design that the firm's stated capability (panel/cohort study, no production ML, no execution infra) can actually build and that a fundamental PM can inspect and challenge end to end, while Plan B piles on IV with a fitted affinity instrument, Driscoll-Kraay/Arellano-Bond/Callaway-Sant'Anna cross-checks and permutation-corrected mechanical regressors that exceed both the team's build capacity and the PM's ability to evaluate credibility.
AB.rationale: The question is a mechanism test (does Kalshi cannibalize DraftKings) whose output is meant to move a position in a named stock for a PM who will ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong — this demands a design that is rigorous but fully legible, not maximally sophisticated. Plan A uses matched control groups, cohort/calendar fixed effects, pre-registered functional forms, a proper MDE power gate before running anything, and negative-control placebos (grocery/fuel spend, pseudo-adoption dates, FanDuel-only pipeline) that a fundamental analyst can walk a PM through step by step; the machinery (wild cluster bootstrap, Poisson PML) is invoked only conditionally, and the core estimator is a standard difference-in-differences the audience can sanity-check on an event-time plot. Plan B is more ambitious but overbuilt for this firm: its primary regressor (Kalshi share of wallet) mechanically contains the outcome, forcing an entire permutation-based correction apparatus just to patch a self-inflicted design flaw that Plan A avoids by studying levels directly; its IV strategy requires fitting a user-level 'affinity' score on a holdout sample (edging into the production-ML territory the firm explicitly rules out) and defending an exogeneity story (national non-sports Kalshi volume) that is not obviously valid and would be hard to defend to an IC; and it runs four to five parallel identification strategies (permutation, IV, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Arellano-Bond, out-of-sample refit) that a 3-person data team plus one engineer will struggle to build, maintain, and reconcile within a 6-18 month decision horizon. Plan B's added rigor (wallet-accounting decomposition, take-rate conversion to revenue, FD symmetry check) is genuinely useful and slightly ahead on connecting deposits to economic impact, but the marginal value does not justify the added complexity and reduced legibility for this audience. Given a concentrated single/paired-name bet where a false positive (wrongly shorting DKNG on an illusory substitution effect) is costly and undiversifiable, the tenet that decides this is fit to the firm's evaluative capacity and build capacity, not raw statistical ambition.

Reliance on card/ACH descriptors will understate Kalshi/DK exposure routed through brokerage or wallet intermediaries, similar to the gap Plan B explicitly quantifies
Matching on pre-period DraftKings intensity could still leave residual selection on unobserved user-level shocks coincident with adoption
issues_with_loser: Primary regressor (Kalshi share of total wallet) mechanically embeds the outcome, requiring an elaborate permutation-null patch rather than avoiding the problem by design

IV instrument (affinity × national non-sports volume) rests on an exogeneity assumption that is asserted rather than strongly defended, and the affinity score's holdout-fitting procedure edges toward the production-ML capability the firm says it will not build

Five-plus parallel estimation strategies (IV, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Arellano-Bond, ppmlhdfe, permutation) exceed what a 3-person data team and one engineer can build, validate, and maintain, and make the final result harder for an IC to defend or falsify quickly

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B delivers a single, PM-legible cohort/event-time design with a built-in breakdown bound answering 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong,' while Plan A stacks IV, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Arellano-Bond, permutation inference and PPML into a multi-method arbitration scheme that exceeds what a 3-person data team, one engineer, and a fundamental PM can build, execute, or evaluate for conviction.
BA.rationale: Both plans attack the same well-posed cannibalization question and both do real work on descriptor hygiene, placebos, pre-trends, and wallet accounting -- this is close. But the firm is a fundamental long/short shop that explicitly can run 'a panel study or a cohort analysis,' has no production-ML build capacity, and needs output a PM can defend by naming what would make it wrong. Plan A reads like it was written for a systematic/quant desk: it layers an instrumented model (affinity x national volume, fit on a holdout, judged by Kleigergen-Paap F-stats) whose exclusion restriction is itself questionable, a staggered-adoption Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator that must be reconciled with the IV result within 2x or deferred to, Arellano-Bond and Driscoll-Kraay corrections, and 1,000-draw permutation inference -- machinery that adds real researcher degrees of freedom and cannot be evaluated by the PM asking naive gut-check questions. It reaches for the sophisticated method before showing the simple one fails, and 'ppmlhdfe leads' is itself a violation of simplest-first for this audience. Plan B keeps one pre-registered primary specification (matched cohort, event-time OLS with user-by-cohort and cohort-by-calendar FE), reports Poisson and other forms as secondary corroboration rather than competing arbiters, and -- crucially -- operationalizes the falsification requirement directly: a partial-identification breakdown value M stating how large the post-trend must be relative to pre-period noise before the confidence set excludes zero, which is exactly the 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' answer a PM can hold in his head. Its matching diagnostics (SMDs, held-out FanDuel and discretionary-spend balance checks) and event-time plot are inspectable early, letting a toxic branch be pruned before the robustness suite is run. Given the concentrated, name-specific use of this output (position sizing on DraftKings), Type I risk is real and both plans build serious defenses against it -- but Plan A's added rigor is diminishing-returns machinery relative to its cost and legibility, whereas Plan B's design is proportionate: rigorous enough to defend a sizing call, simple enough that the team can actually execute and the PM can actually interrogate it.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question actually asked (ARR on MAU, directly) using panel econometrics the firm is equipped to run, while Plan B reframes the primary claim around seat-growth and builds a ridge-regression nowcast with nested CV and empirical-Bayes shrinkage — closer to the production-ML the firm explicitly will not build.
AB.rationale: Both plans are competent and share good instincts: multiple simple baselines, point-in-time data discipline, structural-break screening, consensus-relative scoring, and pre-committed thresholds. The decisive split is firm fit and target fidelity. The mandate says this fund can run panel/cohort studies and buys web/transaction data, but will not build production ML, and needs output a PM can interrogate on a 6-18mo, position-sizing basis. Plan A stays inside classical panel econometrics (fixed effects, unit-root/cointegration diagnostics, clustering/bootstrap SEs) — sophisticated but recognizable machinery for a fundamental shop's quant-adjacent capability, and it regresses log ARR (the actual target) on log MAU directly, exactly the question posed. Its falsification test — refitting on the excluded consumption-metered names and requiring equal performance to sink the thesis — is a genuine negative control derived from the plan's own mechanism, which is exactly the kind of check tenet 9 wants and which Plan B lacks in comparable form. Plan B is intellectually elegant — gating a seat-proxy claim before conditionally building an ARR nowcast is good sequencing in principle — but its secondary stage (pooled fixed-effects ridge, nested-CV tuned penalty, empirical-Bayes shrinkage, Clark-West/DM with HLN correction, 2,000-draw block bootstrap) is a small forecasting-model build that exceeds what a 3-person data team and one engineer at a fundamental L/S shop should be tasked with maintaining, and it drifts the primary claim from ARR to seat-growth, an adjacent quantity, before circling back to ARR only conditionally. That is a real, if partial, goal/target substitution relative to the question as framed. Given breadth here is modest (35-60 names) and the output must be defensible to a PM in plain terms, the more direct, more operationally proportionate design wins.
issues_with_winner: CIPS/Westerlund/wild-bootstrap toolkit is still a lot of econometric machinery for a fundamental PM to sign off on without translation
Three ARR-tier definitions splice/truncated within one series adds researcher discretion that needs to be shown, not just described
Horizon choice (h=0,1,2) selected partly on out-of-sample performance invites some specification search despite the rolling-origin gate
issues_with_loser: Primary gated claim is about seat growth, not ARR, which is what was actually asked, so the headline answer is one step removed from the mandate

No comparably clean negative-control falsification (e.g., testing on categories where the mechanism should fail) analogous to Plan A's consumption-metered refit

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A gates the whole study behind a bespoke, labor-intensive 'seat-disclosure' dataset (hand-mapping ADP pays-per-control, Paycom clients×employees, Dayforce live customers, Wayback-scraped tier prices, etc.) that a 3-person data team and one engineer cannot realistically build in reasonable time and that yields too thin an N to support the very tight thresholds (β∈[0.5,1.5], partial corr ≥0.45, block-bootstrap significance) it then imposes, whereas Plan B uses a fixed, checkable universe rule (>70% seat-metered revenue) and vendor panels the firm already licenses, reaching a testable, decision-relevant result with a genuine mechanism-derived negative control (consumption-priced names) at comparable rigor and far lower upfront cost.
BA.rationale: Both plans are technically excellent and arguably over-instrumented for a fundamental long/short shop's typical audience (Driscoll-Kraay SEs, Clark-West, cointegration tests, wild-cluster bootstraps), so neither wins cleanly on tenet 2's 'audience can evaluate the method' clause — this is a wash. The decisive difference is feasibility and sequencing. Plan A's intellectually appealing mechanism decomposition (MAU→seats→ARR via accounting identity) requires constructing an idiosyncratic 'gate sample' of seat-disclosing companies (payroll/HR names like ADP, Paycom, Dayforce mixed with collaboration-tool names like Atlassian, Asana, Smartsheet) via hand-collected, heterogeneous disclosures and scraped pricing pages. This is exactly the kind of expensive, bespoke data build the tenets caution against committing to before a cheap version has shown the idea is worth pursuing — and it front-loads the most expensive part of the plan rather than the most decisive/cheapest kill test. Worse, the resulting sample is almost certainly too small to support the very demanding statistical thresholds Plan A itself requires (tight beta bounds, partial correlation floors, bootstrap significance, leave-one-out stability), risking a plan that cannot pass its own gate for reasons unrelated to whether the hypothesis is true. Plan B instead defines a clean, rule-based universe (~35-60 names, seat-metered >70% of revenue, standard hostname convention) using data types the firm already buys (web/app panels), reaching ~900-1,000 company-quarters — enough power for the panel methods it proposes — and folds in a real negative control derived from its own mechanism (refitting on excluded consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis), which is exactly the falsification tenet 9 wants, at no extra data cost. Plan B's benchmarks (naive carry-forward, trailing growth, two-way FE without MAU) are also simpler and more legible to a PM than Plan A's variance-decomposition-plus-ridge-plus-empirical-Bayes pipeline. Plan A's mechanism-first instinct is good practice in principle, but as executed it inverts the 'cheapest, most decisive test first' ordering by making the expensive, hard-to-build piece the prerequisite gate.
issues_with_winner: Still carries fairly heavy panel econometrics (unit-root/cointegration tests, wild-cluster bootstrap) that may exceed what the investment staff can independently evaluate, even if the data team can run it

Front-loads the most expensive, hardest-to-verify data construction rather than the cheapest test that could kill the idea early

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B validates actual identification correctness against a held-out ground-truth set with a precision-calibrated abstain rule matched to the stated catastrophic cost of a confident wrong match, while Plan A validates only cluster cohesion and stability and never tests whether a named match is actually correct.
AB.rationale: The firm's explicit failure mode is a confident wrong match sizing a position on the wrong bank's customers — this is a Type-I-dominant setting where the burden of proof must fall on precision of the specific ID-to-institution assignment, not on the internal quality of a clustering. Plan A builds an elaborate unsupervised pipeline (Ward/GMM/HDBSCAN ensembles, co-association, PCA) and validates it with silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, bootstrap Jaccard stability, and cross-window ARI — all of which measure whether clusters are cohesive and reproducible, not whether the eventual name attached to a cluster is correct. Its naming step (Hungarian rank-matching with margin gates) is confirmatory but untested against any ground truth, so a systematic swap between two similar-archetype, similar-size banks in the same country would sail through every gate undetected — precisely the failure mode the PM most fears. Plan B instead treats identification as a calibrated decision problem: it builds a (small but real) labeled validation set (consented survey, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases), holds out at the institution level (not just customers) via nested leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out CV, and only accepts a match at a pre-committed 95% precision threshold with an explicit abstain sink otherwise. It also runs genuine falsification tests baked into the design — permuted fingerprints must score at chance, phantom IDs must abstain, dropping the largest comparator must degrade gracefully — which directly answers 'what would make this wrong' rather than only reporting internal consistency. B also sequences for information: it pilots the easiest market (concentrated NL) first and pre-commits to stopping if that fails, rather than running the full multi-country pipeline before any go/no-go, and it puts a governance/GDPR gate at the very front, which A never addresses despite working with anonymized personal transaction data — a material omission for a real fund's legal and compliance exposure. Both plans are technically sophisticated and demand real infrastructure, but B pairs its sophistication with a metric (deposit-volume-weighted held-out precision) that is directly interpretable by a PM and directly tied to the risk that matters, whereas A's cluster-quality metrics are one step removed from the actual claim being made.
issues_with_winner: Ground-truth validation set is very small (25–60 per country, unusable below 15), so precision estimates themselves carry wide uncertainty
Heavy reliance on many disparate national regulatory, tariff, and benefit-calendar sources is a large data-engineering lift for a 3-person data team plus one engineer

Sinkhorn/Metropolis marginals and conformal calibration add real statistical machinery that may be hard for non-quant investment staff to independently audit without a simpler corroborating check surfaced to the PM
issues_with_loser: Validates cluster cohesion and stability but never tests whether the final named match is actually correct against any ground truth, which is precisely the risk the firm cares most about
Naming step is confirmatory (rubric plus margin gates) without any held-out accuracy check, so a plausible but wrong match between similar peer banks would pass all stated gates
No governance/GDPR checkpoint despite operating on anonymized retail transaction data, a material omission given the firm's stated privacy-sensitive panel
Runs the full multi-country, multi-hundred-institution pipeline before any early stop/kill checkpoint, rather than piloting the easiest case first to fail fast cheaply

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A builds the false-confident-match risk directly into the design — precision calibrated to 95% via Venn-Abers/conformal, an abstain sink, and validation against real ground-truth labels (consented survey, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases) — while Plan B's final named-institution step relies only on internal cluster-stability metrics with no comparable external check on whether the name assigned is actually correct.
BA.rationale: The PM explicitly named the failure mode that matters: a confident wrong match, because it means sizing a position on the wrong bank's customers. That makes this a Type-I-dominant problem, and the winning plan has to be judged mainly on how well it controls and measures the false-positive rate on the specific deliverable the fund needs — a named, ticker-mapped institution, not a cluster label. Plan A's entire scoring and validation apparatus is built around that: a pre-committed 95%-precision criterion with per-country kill thresholds, an abstain/UNKNOWN sink with explicit reason codes, quarter-versioned anchors to handle bank mergers, leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out nested CV, and — crucially — external ground-truth labels (survey respondents, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases) used specifically to check whether the named assignment is correct, not just internally consistent. That last piece is what a skeptical PM asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' actually wants to see. Plan B is a genuinely well-sequenced capability build — its country→archetype→name ladder is cheaper to kill early and more tractable for a small data team using standard clustering tools rather than optimal-transport machinery — and its cluster-level validation (bootstrap stability, permutation nulls, four-window ARI) is excellent. But its most important step, named-institution assignment, is validated only by rank-correlation heuristics and internal margin thresholds; there is no external label check on whether the name given is actually right, which is precisely the failure mode the desk cares about. Plan B's honest fallback to 'country and archetype only' is a legitimate scientific answer but does not give the desk what it needs to size a position, whereas Plan A pushes all the way to the deliverable and tells you, per institution, when it doesn't have enough evidence to trust the answer. That direct alignment between the plan's central risk-control mechanism and the PM's stated central fear is the deciding factor.
issues_with_winner: Building anchors across ECB/Bundesbank/DNB/Banco de España/Banca d'Italia/ACPR/KNF/EBA plus tariff booklets and benefit-calendar rules for five countries is a large data-acquisition burden for a 3-person data team plus one engineer, and the plan does not clearly stage this so that only the Netherlands anchors are built before the pilot go/no-go

the scoring machinery (min-cost flow, Sinkhorn marginals, Jonker-Volgenant assignment, Venn-Abers calibration) is sophisticated enough that a PM will need the log-likelihood component breakdown, not the aggregate score, to actually evaluate a specific match — the plan should make that decomposition the primary reporting unit, not an afterthought

committing to full fine-grained anchor collection for fragmented markets (DE/AT/IT) before any market-level pilot evidence that fine signals resolve the 350-Sparkassen problem risks sunk cost if those markets simply aren't identifiable
issues_with_loser: the final and most business-critical step — naming a specific institution — is validated only by rank-agreement and margin thresholds internal to the method, with no external ground-truth check comparable to Plan A's survey/provider-seed labels, which is a real gap given that a wrong confident name is the stated failure mode

the explicit acceptable fallback of 'country and archetype only' does not satisfy the actual business need (attaching behavioral data to a specific ticker to size a position), so a technically successful run of this plan can still fail to deliver anything the desk can trade on

AB.key_differentiator: Plan A requires building a proprietary 40-60 case cross-strata comparables database with a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework and vendor datasets (DealScan, Infralogic, Bloomberg CACS/DDIS) that a two-analyst desk with no quant staff and no dataset-building capacity cannot construct, evaluate, or maintain, whereas Plan B relies on the primary documents, filings, and expert-network channel checks the firm actually has, sequenced cheapest-kill-first toward a dated, trade-ready verdict.
AB.rationale: Both plans correctly frame this as a single-situation mispricing question with a sound H1/H2/H3 taxonomy and pre-registered falsifiers, so tenet 1 is roughly a wash. The split comes on firm fit and sequencing. This desk consumes filings, sell-side, and expert calls; it has no quant research staff and cannot build datasets. Plan A's methodology section is built around coding 40-60 comparable SPV releases across three strata, licensing project-finance and loan databases, and deriving a formal prior with an explicit likelihood-ratio threshold ('20:1-30:1 against H1, ~25x LR needed') - a base rate asserted with false precision before any such database exists, which is invented statistical machinery this audience cannot build or sanity-check, and it front-loads that architecture before the cheap disconfirming checks. Plan B instead leans on the resource this desk actually has - expert-network-style channel checks (counsel, syndicate desk, ex-bankers, OSATs, EDA/IP teams, rival foundry) - uses a small, feasible same-vintage comparable set (5-10 SPVs) rather than a constructed database, explicitly says to check the price reaction first, and states H1 only survives if H2/H3 die via the cheapest disconfirmation. That is exactly the entropy-reducing, adaptive sequencing the framework rewards, and it ends in a trade-sizing step consistent with an event-driven desk whose risk manager cuts positions fast. Plan A's rigor is real but calibrated for a shop with quant infrastructure this platform does not have; Plan B gets to an actionable, inspectable verdict faster using tools this specific desk can actually operate.
issues_with_winner: EL/notional bridge and rating-shadowing sizing section is still fairly quantitative for a document-and-expert-network shop, though it is paired with a simple cross-check (SPV spread vs hyperscaler/CDS curve) that the audience can verify
Long list of confounders (antitrust, FX review, export control, transfer pricing) risks diffusing focus if not tightly gated by the stated kill criteria
issues_with_loser: Requires building a 40-60 case coded comparables database across three strata plus subscriptions to DealScan/Infralogic/Bloomberg CACS-DDIS - infrastructure and analyst-time this two-person, no-quant-staff desk cannot sustain
Asserts a specific prior base rate and likelihood-ratio bar ('20:1-30:1', '~25x LR needed') before the comparables set is actually built, which is invented precision dressed as an empirical prior
Buries the cheap, high-value checks (e.g., price reaction, consent solicitation) behind a heavy base-rate and portfolio-sweep architecture rather than sequencing the decisive, low-cost tests first
Monthly-counted hiring-req tracking and conference-paper mining resemble a signal-research build more suited to a systematic desk than a fast single-name event catalyst call

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B answers 'how often does this kind of release mean strategic risk-transfer on average' by building a 40-60 case, multi-jurisdiction comparables database, which is both a different question than 'is this specific SPV mispriced now' and infrastructure this two-analyst, no-dataset-capacity desk cannot build in a weeks-to-months catalyst window; Plan A stays inside the single situation's own documents and expert channels and ends in a sized trade.
BA.rationale: The brief is explicit: this desk has no quant staff, no capacity to build datasets, consumes filings/sell-side/expert calls, and cares whether THIS situation is mispriced now, not whether an effect holds on average. Plan B's methodology section requires coding 40-60 comparable SPV releases across three strata, pulling original-language filings from TWSE, DART, EDINET, Companies House, Irish CRO, Luxembourg RCS, Dutch KvK and Cayman registries, and computing a prior odds/likelihood-ratio (20:1-30:1, ~25x LR needed) to judge the residual. That is a dataset-construction and quantitative-inference exercise the firm has explicitly said it cannot staff or run, and it answers a base-rate question rather than the specific-situation question asked. It would also blow through the weeks-to-months trading horizon before producing anything actionable. Plan A, by contrast, works almost entirely inside the SPV's own document set (LLC agreement, guaranty, supply/capacity agreements, ASC 460/810 notes), sizes a pre/post notional and EL bridge specific to this deal, and corroborates the second-source hypothesis through the exact channels this desk already has (counsel, syndicate desk, ex-planners, OSATs, expert calls) — with a lightweight 5-10 case base-rate check rather than a 40-60 case database, proportionate to what two analysts can actually do. It sequences cheapest disconfirmation first (release language, consent solicitation, EL delta) before the effortful qualification corroboration, and ends with a trade sized to the weakest link — output the PM can act on. Plan B is more statistically rigorous in the abstract, but rigor calibrated to a systematic-signal audience is a defect, not a strength, when the audience is a concentrated single-name book that needs a judgeable verdict on one situation fast.
issues_with_winner: Document list is very long and could still overwhelm two analysts if not triaged; relies on the stated 'cheapest disconfirmation first' discipline actually being followed.
Second-source corroboration network (counsel, syndicate desk, ex-planners, OSATs, EDA/IP teams, rival foundry) is itself a lot of expert-call legwork to run inside a weeks-to-months window.
issues_with_loser: Requires building and coding a 40-60 case comparables database across numerous foreign-language registries, which this firm has no capacity or quant staff to execute.

Reframes the question from 'is this specific situation mispriced' into 'what is the base rate of strategic vs mechanical SPV releases,' which is the wrong target for a single-name event-driven mandate.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B checks whether the signal is already sold or arbitraged (vendor landscape scan, McLean-Pontiff decay prior, 2004-2010 replication) and pre-registers a single cheap specification with a 14-day kill gate before committing to any build, whereas Plan A commits to a full domain-adapted transformer pipeline and quarter-scale build before ever asking whether the effect is incremental to what the street and vendors already have.
AB.rationale: For a systematic firm whose stated failure modes are crowding, cost, and capacity, the first-order question is not 'can we measure tone precisely' but 'is there anything left to find and can it survive costs' — Plan B attacks that directly with a half-day vendor crowding survey and a literature-grounded prior on decay, then locks a simple LM-based, pre-registered specification with explicit, falsifiable kill criteria (t-threshold, net spread/IR, year and size-quartile consistency, placebo and shuffle tests, vendor rank-correlation as a duplication check) reachable in about two weeks. That is exactly the entropy-reducing, adaptive sequencing the setting calls for: the branch that kills the idea sits at the front, and the expensive infrastructure build (days 11-14, or licensing) is conditional on passing, not sunk regardless of outcome. Plan A is methodologically excellent and well within this firm's ML capability, but it builds the full domain-adapted DeBERTa pipeline, annotation process, and multi-stage validation suite before any cheap check establishes the effect isn't already priced or vendor-sold; LM/FinBERT appear only as an ablation baseline inside a fully built pipeline rather than as the gating first step. It also never asks whether S&P, RavenPack, or Bigdata already sells this, despite crowding being named as this firm's central risk. Both plans use appropriately strict, multiple-testing-aware thresholds suited to a systematic shop that runs many specifications; the difference is Plan B reaches a stop/build decision an order of magnitude faster and cheaper, and that decision is genuinely conditional (pass triggers a build-vs-license comparison, fail triggers a two-page memo naming the likely residual channel), which is what separates a research plan from a task list here.

The vendor rank-correlation crowding check (>0.7 kills it) assumes point-in-time vendor histories are available and comparable, which may not hold cleanly
issues_with_loser: Commits to building a full domain-adapted transformer, annotation pipeline, and silver-labeling process before any cheap test (including its own LM/FinBERT baseline) has shown the effect survives basic controls, violating simplest-first sequencing

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A tests the simplest tone measure (LM dictionary) first with a hard pre-registered gate and only escalates to infrastructure/vendor licensing if it clears, while Plan B commits weeks of annotation, codebook design, and domain-adaptive transformer training before ever checking whether a cheap baseline shows anything.
BA.rationale: Both plans are well-matched to a systematic firm's capability and vocabulary — point-in-time data, peer-relative construction, factor-neutral portfolios, HLZ-style multiple-testing correction, cost/capacity/crowding framing. AB.rationale:
The question asked is squarely single-name: is this specific company's margin risk from this vendor renegotiation understated. Plan A takes that at face value, correctly discards management tone as confounded by the negotiation itself, and substitutes a concrete, bottoms-up/top-down spend estimate, contract-mechanics read, vendor-behavior comparables, and a sensitivity table that converts directly into bps of margin and EPS impact — exactly the currency an investment committee needs. Every input (10-K purchase obligations, ASC 350-40/985-20 notes, material contracts exhibits, vendor price lists) is something one analyst can pull from Bloomberg/EDGAR without new infrastructure, and the plan is sequenced so the decisive question (is the dollar exposure even material) comes before the more subtle contract-mechanics and vendor-comparable work — a kill criterion is present and cheap to reach. It also self-corrects for the survivorship problem (bad renewals go unpublicized) by inflating the assumed severity for high-switching-cost customers, and it separates 'immaterial' from 'not uncomfortable,' avoiding false reassurance. This is a plan built for a concentrated, long-horizon, business-risk-focused shop.

Plan B is a well-constructed piece of systematic NLP research — pre-registration, placebo topics, out-of-sample splits, Romano-Wolf corrections, block bootstraps, elastic-net weights, two vendors of transcripts, Visible Alpha/IBES/CRSP/Compustat panels — but almost none of it is something this firm can build, run, or even sanity-check. There are no engineers or data scientists, no one who maintains a database, and the IC explicitly distrusts models it cannot inspect; a κ≥0.70 LLM classifier trained on 1,000 hand labels and a 40,000 firm-quarter panel regression is the opposite of inspectable to this audience. It also answers a different question: it is a capability-build for a generalizable evasiveness-as-signal factor, not a determination of whether this company's margins are at more risk than guided. Even in its 'success' branch, the deliverable is a cross-sectional predictive score, not a number this PM can put in a model for this position. The publishable-null framing ('H1 true, H2 false is the modal outcome') is honest but underlines that the plan is optimized to learn about a factor, not to resolve the concentrated position in front of the committee this quarter.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A builds a cross-sectional NLP signal-validation research program (40,000 firm-quarter panel, hand-labeled classifiers, elastic-net, Driscoll-Kraay SEs, multiple vendor datasets) to test whether evasiveness predicts margin surprises broadly, which is not the question asked and not something this five-person shop can build or maintain, whereas Plan B directly sizes this specific vendor renegotiation's margin exposure using filings, contract mechanics, and comparable-renewal data with one analyst and Excel.
BA.rationale: The question is single-name: is this company's defensiveness a real near-term margin risk. Plan A answers a different, broader question entirely — it treats the single observation as a launchpad for a generalizable evasiveness-predicts-margins signal, complete with pre-registration, placebo topics, Romano-Wolf multiple-comparison correction, and out-of-sample splits. That is a capability-build/broad-market-effect research program, not an answer to 'is this company's margin at risk.' Even if flawlessly executed, it produces a cross-sectional base rate, not a verdict on this business, and the firm has no engineers, no data scientists, and no one who maintains a database to build or sustain the transcript-NLP-panel infrastructure it requires. It is unexecutable and unusable for this client, and it is also not what was asked. Plan B correctly identifies that tone is confounded by the negotiation itself and is near-worthless, then substitutes a testable, mechanistic question: how large is the licence spend, what do the contract terms allow, what has this vendor done to comparables, and what did management say versus what happened last time. It sizes the risk in dollars and margin bps, inverts the sensitivity table to identify what magnitude of uplift would actually matter, and validates against the firm's own renewal history — all using Bloomberg, filings, and public vendor pricing data, fully within what one analyst can execute and an IC can inspect line by line. It also correctly identifies the asymmetric tail case (single-source, metric-change step function) that tone-reading would never surface. This is a case where goal mismatch and firm fit both point the same direction decisively.

response.plan_implied_asker: A fundamental long/short shop with an alt-data panel team that wants a causally defensible read on a specific competitive-substitution story to size a named position, not a cross-sectional signal desk
response.what_would_falsify: A rejected pre-trend joint F-test (β₋₆..β₋₂ not flat), a partial-identification breakdown value M close to the plan's own disqualifying bound (M≈0.5, i.e. a plausible pre-existing trend alone explains the post-period gap), or placebo channels (grocery/fuel/e-commerce spend, pseudo-adoption six months earlier, first-transaction-at-an-unrelated-merchant, the FanDuel-only pipeline) showing a comparable 'effect' — any of these is pre-committed as grounds to treat the substitution claim as not established.

issues.summary: The plan never states what the market (sell-side notes, DraftKings' own earnings-call commentary on prediction markets) already believes about Kalshi cannibalization, so a clean causal result may only confirm a thesis that is already in the multiple.
issues.why_it_applies_here: DraftKings management and sell-side analysts have already publicly discussed event-contract competition; the panel gives a genuine measurement edge (magnitude and timing ahead of reported financials), but the plan doesn't say whether the magnitude it expects to find is larger or smaller than what's implicitly priced, which is the difference between an investable finding and a well-executed confirmation of consensus.
issues.what_breaks: The PM step where the finding is translated into a position-size change: a statistically airtight β with no view on what was already assumed by the market gives no basis for sizing up or down.
issues.fix: Add one paragraph benchmarking the expected/found effect size against what sell-side models or DraftKings' own disclosed guidance already imply for prediction-market drag, so the causal estimate can be read as incremental or not.

issues.summary: DraftKings 'wallet share' (a secondary/cross-check outcome) falls mechanically once Kalshi dollars enter the denominator of total wallet, independent of any true reduction in DraftKings spend.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The moment a user has any Kalshi debit, total wallet = DraftKings + Kalshi + other by construction, so wallet share for that user-month declines even if DraftKings dollars are literally unchanged; this is the definitional-relationship failure mode, not a substitution measurement.
issues.what_breaks: If the primary dollars/retention estimates come back weak or ambiguous, the wallet-share cross-check could be read as corroborating substitution when it is guaranteed to move in that direction by definition.
issues.fix: Either drop wallet-share as corroborating evidence or restate it as a share of DraftKings-plus-other-sportsbook spend only (excluding Kalshi from the denominator), so it isn't tautologically responsive to adoption.

issues.summary: Because retail-scale event-contract sports trading on Kalshi only recently expanded, the adopter cohort studied is necessarily an early, possibly unrepresentative slice, while the fund's decision horizon (6-18 months) spans a period where adoption composition will likely broaden.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The robustness list itself flags dropping Nov 2024/Jan 2025 cohorts, which signals that a meaningful share of usable post-period data sits right at the recency edge — the population available to study is disproportionately the earliest, most engaged adopters, not the mainstream user the DraftKings thesis over the next 6-18 months depends on.
issues.what_breaks: External validity of the estimated β for sizing a position meant to hold over the next 6-18 months, if early adopters substitute more (or less) aggressively than the broader base that will follow.
issues.fix: Report the effect separately by adoption-cohort vintage (early vs. later within the sample) to see whether the estimated substitution is stable or an early-adopter artifact before extrapolating it forward.

issues.summary: The event-time window is fixed at -6..+6 months, so the study can speak to the lower end of the fund's 6-18 month horizon but says nothing about whether substitution persists, fades, or grows over the back half of that horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Position sizing decisions on DraftKings implicitly bet on a directional trend holding for up to 18 months, but the design as specified stops observing three months short of that, and doesn't state a plan to re-run or extend the window as more post-period months accrue.
issues.what_breaks: A PM sizing a multi-quarter short/underweight based on a 6-month substitution estimate has no evidence on whether the effect is durable or a novelty-driven transient that reverses by month 12.
issues.fix: Pre-commit to a follow-up re-estimation at +12 (and ideally +18) once enough cohorts have matured, rather than treating the +6 window as the final answer.

response.overall: This is a well-built plan: the taxonomy, matching, event-study design, placebos, pre-trend and partial-identification checks, and explicit pre-commitment give the PM exactly the falsification handles the brief asks for, and the scope matches what a data team plus one engineer can actually run without new infrastructure. The remaining gaps are secondary polish, not structural — tie the finding back to what's already priced/discussed about Kalshi-DraftKings substitution, stop treating wallet share as independent corroborating evidence given its mechanical construction, check whether the studied adopters are representative of the wave still to come, and plan to extend the observation window toward the 18-month end of the fund's horizon.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. Legitimate desk-level concern for this firm: output must change position sizing and be defensible to a PM, and the plan is silent on what magnitude is already priced given DraftKings management and sell-side have publicly discussed event-contract competition. Grounded in the specific situation rather than a generic 'is there edge' recital.

Not in gold but a sharp, plan-specific point: the plan lists DraftKings wallet share and total wallet including Kalshi as secondary outcomes and also uses wallet share as a seasonality cross-check, and that ratio falls mechanically once Kalshi dollars enter the denominator. This is a genuine definitional-circularity risk in a stated cross-check, not a canned objection.

Adjacent to gold blocking#2 but a distinct objection (external validity of early-adopter composition for a 6-18 month hold, rather than pooling politically-driven and sports-driven regimes). It is anchored to a real feature of the plan (the Nov 2024/Jan 2025 cohort-drop robustness and the recency edge of usable post-period data), so it is a defensible unlisted concern rather than a match; borderline against being a softer restatement of the reviewer's timing point.

Not in gold. Specific to the plan's fixed -6..+6 window and its +1..+3 / +4..+6 aggregation against the fund's stated six-to-eighteen-month horizon; the plan indeed offers no persistence evidence past month six and no re-run/extension protocol. Legitimate for a PM sizing a multi-quarter position.

response.plan_implied_asker: An applied-micro/causal-inference research team with dedicated econometric staff and infrastructure to build and maintain IV, GMM and matching pipelines — not a PM-facing fundamental shop; the plan assumes an audience that can evaluate Kleibergen-Paap statistics and Arellano-Bond bias on its own terms.
response.what_would_falsify: H1 is dead if β is statistically indistinguishable from the permuted/mechanical null at 5%, if the event-study ATT diverges from β×mean Δshare by more than ~2x (event study wins), if the six pre-trend leads are jointly significant (p ≤ 0.10), or if placebo categories (grocery/streaming/non-legal states/neobank fake-treatment) show effects comparable to the DK result.

issues.summary: The causal-inference stack (holdout-fit IV with Kleibergen-Paap, Arellano-Bond GMM, Callaway-Sant'Anna event study, wild cluster bootstrap) requires econometric specialization the stated 3-person data team and single engineer do not have and cannot maintain.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This exact team profile (a licensing/cleaning data team plus one engineer, no dedicated econometrician) is given in the brief, and the ultimate consumer is a PM who will ask 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' in plain terms — a question this stack cannot be answered for without trusting the analyst's black box.
issues.what_breaks: Build risk on the estimation pipeline itself, and downstream, the PM cannot independently interrogate an F-stat or a GMM instrument set, so the sizing decision rests on trust rather than the PM's own judgment.
issues.fix: Make the fixed-effects regression with the permutation null and the event-study cross-check the primary deliverable — both produce PM-checkable outputs (wallet-accounting sum-to-100%, headline $ displaced) — and demote IV/Arellano-Bond to optional robustness only if the primary result is contested, always shown alongside the plain estimate.

issues.summary: The power/MDE calculation, explicitly labeled 'power first,' is textually the last item in Validation rather than the gate that determines whether the rest of the build is worth doing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The clean adopter count here is bounded further by the broker-distributed Kalshi attribution gap (Robinhood/Webull), so the effective N for the cannibalization test could be small; whether the panel can even detect an economically relevant $ displacement is knowable cheaply and should precede the descriptor audits and multi-model build, not follow them in the document.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is sunk into hand-audited descriptor dictionaries, attribution-gap quantification, and multiple model specifications before learning whether the sample supports inference at a size that would move a position.
issues.fix: Run the MDE calculation off raw adopter counts and rough deposit variance before any audit or model-building step; treat a failing MDE as an immediate stop.

issues.summary: The plan never states how a well-identified per-user $-displaced-per-10-points-share estimate gets scaled into DKNG's (and Flutter/FD's) consolidated revenue or margin impact — the number that actually changes position sizing.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The stated deliverable of this work is to change sizing on named companies; a micro coefficient is silent on what share of DK's active base is affected, what share of DK revenue those users represent, and how fast it flows to reported financials — without that bridge the rigorously identified result cannot yet inform a position.
issues.what_breaks: The PM receives a clean causal estimate but still has to guess the firm-level magnitude, reintroducing the kind of unsupported extrapolation the rest of the plan is careful to avoid.
issues.fix: Add an explicit, separately-flagged aggregation step using adopter penetration, the H4 tenure/spend-decile weights, and coverage-adjusted extrapolation to DK's reported base, presented as a range — or state plainly that this study answers the mechanism question only and a follow-on step is required for sizing.

issues.summary: The plan never states what sell-side/consensus already assumes about Kalshi cannibalizing DraftKings spend, so it cannot show the finding is incremental rather than a confirmation of a widely discussed bear thesis.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Prediction-market cannibalization of sportsbooks has been an active bear narrative on DKNG since Kalshi's sports-adjacent contracts launched, discussed on calls and in sell-side notes; a rigorous internal replication of a magnitude the market has already debated is confirmatory unless the panel reveals a magnitude, timing, or cohort concentration (e.g., the H4 high-spend-user result) outside what is already assumed.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean, statistically significant β could support a position the market has already taken, producing no incremental return despite a methodologically correct call.
issues.fix: Before the full build, record the current sell-side range/assumption for this effect (from notes or consensus models) and check whether the design — especially the H4 tenure/spend cut — is positioned to find something outside that range.

response.overall: This is an unusually rigorous, well-specified causal design with genuine falsification logic, pre-registered kill criteria, and sensible negative controls — better disciplined than most plans of this type. Its failure mode is not weak identification but fit: the econometric machinery exceeds what the stated 3-person data team and one engineer can build, maintain, or explain to a PM who must approve sizing off it, the power check that could kill the idea cheaply is buried at the end rather than gating the build, and the plan stops at a per-user causal estimate without saying how that becomes a firm-level revenue view or how it differs from what the market already assumes about Kalshi-DK cannibalization. Trim to the fixed-effects-plus-permutation-null-plus-event-study core, run power first, and add the consensus-benchmark and firm-level aggregation steps before this is actionable.

issue_buckets.why: Not the gold objection (which is about estimand choice and the outcome-in-regressor problem, not staffing), but a defensible desk concern grounded in the stated firm profile: a three-person licensing/cleaning data team plus one engineer, no econometrician, and a PM who must be able to interrogate the result. The plan stacks holdout-fitted IV, Arellano-Bond, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Driscoll-Kraay and wild bootstrap. Marked uncertain because it partially overlaps the gold point about design budget being spent on defending complexity, and because a fundamental fund's analyst could plausibly execute standard panel estimators without dedicated econometric staff.

Partly a document-ordering complaint that the plan itself pre-empts ('Power first' with an explicit MDE formula, design effect and rho range), which pushes toward the canonical sample-size objection. But the specific bite — that the clean adopter count is further eroded by the broker-distributed Kalshi attribution gap (Robinhood/Webull have no descriptor) plus the ≥6 pre/≥6 post and payroll-anchor filters, so effective N for the displacement test may be too small to detect an economically relevant dollar figure — is tied to this plan's own stated gaps and is worth a cheap gate before the descriptor audit and multi-model build. Uncertain because the plan does commit to power first and to quantifying the undercount.

Legitimate and specific to this firm's stated output (change sizing on named companies). The plan converts deposits to revenue at explicit take rates and headlines '$ displaced per 10-point share rise', but never bridges the panel-user coefficient to DKNG/Flutter consolidated revenue: panel-to-population coverage, what share of DK's handle the affected cohort represents, and flow-through timing to reported financials. Without that bridge the PM must improvise the extrapolation the rest of the plan carefully avoids.

Not in gold and not a generic recitation: prediction-market cannibalization of sportsbooks is an actively traded DKNG bear narrative, so the plan needs to state where its finding differs from consensus (magnitude, timing, or the H4 concentration in long-tenured whales) for the work to be incremental at a six-to-eighteen-month horizon. The plan never addresses priced-in expectations at all, so the objection is earned by an actual omission rather than asserted in the abstract.

response.plan_implied_asker: A quant/systematic panel-econometrics team building an academically rigorous cross-sectional signal for its own sake, not a concentrated fundamental long/short PM who needs a fast, name-by-name defensible story.
response.what_would_falsify: Stated null: MAU adds nothing beyond lagged ARR and company trend. Explicit falsifier: refit the same specification on the excluded consumption-priced names (Snowflake, Datadog, MongoDB, Confluent) where the seat-mechanism cannot apply — if MAU predicts their revenue equally well, the thesis is sunk. Also gated on beating a two-way-FE-without-MAU benchmark out of sample via Diebold-Mariano (p<0.05) on rolling-origin and leave-one-company-out splits.

issues.summary: The full panel-econometrics stack (CIPS, Westerlund cointegration, ECM, Driscoll-Kraay, wild-cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD, Bai-Perron) is more machinery than a ~40-cluster panel needs and more than this audience can interrogate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With only ~40 independent company clusters (acknowledged in the plan itself), several of these tests are being pushed near or past the edge of their asymptotic justification, and no PM at a 30-person fundamental shop can push back on a Rademacher wild-cluster bootstrap or a Pesaran CD statistic — the model's credibility ends up resting entirely on the naive benchmarks bolted on for validation, making the econometric layer cost without buying defensibility.
issues.what_breaks: When a PM asks 'why do you believe this,' the analyst's honest answer collapses to the three simple benchmarks (A/B/C) and the MAPE bar — the sophisticated middle layer adds fragility (more places to have made a coding error) without adding anything the PM can independently check.
issues.fix: Keep one robust inference method (within estimator + either Driscoll-Kraay or wild-cluster bootstrap, not both) and drop the unit-root/cointegration/ECM branch unless the level-form result actually fails; let the naive-benchmark beat-test carry the argument, as designed.

issues.summary: The plan commits to full multi-vendor data licensing, two-source reconciliation, break-detection and event-logging across 35–60 names before any cheap check of whether the correlation exists at all.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Several names in the universe (Atlassian, Salesforce, HubSpot, Workday) have years of disclosed ARR and long-available web-traffic panels; a same-week scatter of published MAU growth against disclosed ARR growth for 8-10 of these would tell you the sign and rough magnitude of β before any spend on the second MAU vendor, the Wayback pricing scrape, or the break-detection pipeline.
issues.what_breaks: All of the licensing and reconciliation cost is sunk before the first falsification checkpoint (the consumption-priced-names test) is reached, so a null result arrives only after the expensive part is already built.
issues.fix: Run a 5-10 name pilot on one MAU source and disclosed ARR only; confirm sign, rough magnitude, and that it beats the naive carry-forward benchmark before scaling to the full 35-60 name, two-vendor build.

issues.summary: The price/mix-drift control (Wayback pricing-page snapshots) captures list price, which is not the realized price actually paid by the largest, most heavily-covered names in the sample.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, and Adobe negotiate custom, heavily discounted enterprise pricing that never appears on a public pricing page, while the SMB self-serve names (Zoom, RingCentral, HubSpot) do have list prices that approximate what's paid — so the exact control meant to separate 'logins changed' from 'price changed' is blind precisely for the enterprise-heavy tail of the sample, which is also where position sizes are largest.
issues.what_breaks: For enterprise names, ARR growth driven by negotiated discount or mix changes will be silently misattributed to MAU (or a real null will be masked by uncontrolled price movement), corrupting β exactly where the trading decision has the most capital behind it.
issues.fix: Split the sample by GTM motion (self-serve/list-priced vs. enterprise-negotiated) and report β and validation metrics separately, or substitute a realized-ASP proxy (RPO-per-customer, disclosed average deal size) for the enterprise subset instead of list price.

issues.summary: The plan never addresses whether MAU/app-usage panels are already inside sell-side consensus for these names, so beating a naive random-walk or FE-without-MAU benchmark does not establish the signal is unpriced.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Web-traffic-based SaaS revenue prediction using Similarweb/Sensor Tower-style panels is one of the most widely distributed alt-data theses in the industry, and Visible Alpha contributors covering these exact heavily-followed names plausibly already reference similar usage trackers when setting their ARR numbers — the plan's primary pass/fail gate (beats two-way FE without MAU, via Diebold-Mariano) is a much lower bar than beating what's already in the price, and only the secondary growth-terms check (below cross-analyst dispersion in ≥60% of quarters) actually engages consensus.
issues.what_breaks: A pass on the primary DM-test criterion could still mean the information is already fully reflected in consensus and price, so sizing a position off it risks trading an already-priced view even though the statistical test 'succeeds.'
issues.fix: Promote the consensus-beating check to the primary success criterion (not a secondary growth-terms gate), and add a short diagnostic characterizing whether the sell-side's own estimate revisions already correlate with the public MAU series before claiming the finding is actionable.

response.overall: The design is unusually careful about confounds — price/mix drift, shelfware asymmetry, tracker rebasing, panel composition, and a genuine negative control on consumption-priced names — and states a real falsifier and null. But it is built at a sophistication and scope that exceeds what a concentrated fundamental long/short shop needs or can independently evaluate, it spends most of its cost before a cheap pilot could have confirmed or killed the premise, its price-drift control silently fails exactly where enterprise pricing dominates the sample, and it never checks whether the alt-data signal is already inside sell-side consensus for these heavily-covered names. None of this is fatal — a pilot-first, price-motion-split, consensus-anchored version of the same plan would answer the question faster and more defensibly.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold, but a legitimate, plan-specific critique: it uses the plan's own admission of ~40 effective clusters and the firm's stated defensibility constraint (PM asking what would have to be true) to argue the CIPS/Westerlund/ECM/Driscoll-Kraay/wild-bootstrap/CD layer is beyond both its asymptotic warrant and the audience's ability to interrogate. This is earned against this plan's specific machinery, not a generic 'too complex' recital.

Legitimate sequencing objection tied to this plan: it names companies with long disclosed-ARR histories (Atlassian, Salesforce, HubSpot, Workday) where a cheap scatter would establish sign and magnitude of β before committing to second-vendor licensing, Wayback pricing scrapes, break detection and event logs. Fits the firm's small data team/one-engineer constraint and is not a canned objection.

Sharp, plan-specific measurement critique the reviewer did not list: the plan's chosen price control is Wayback pricing-page snapshots, which capture list price only, and the evaluator correctly identifies that this control is blind exactly for the enterprise-negotiated names (Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Adobe) that would carry the largest positions, while working for the SMB self-serve names. It bites on the specific control the plan proposes.

'No edge / already priced' is a canonical objection, but here it is at least partly earned: the plan's primary pass/fail gate is a Diebold-Mariano win over a two-way FE model with no MAU, which is indeed a statistical-accuracy bar rather than an information-advantage bar, and the evaluator correctly notes the consensus-dispersion criterion is relegated to a secondary growth-terms check. Weakened by the fact that the plan does include the cross-analyst dispersion comparison and expects edge to concentrate in smaller-cap names, so the point is closer to a re-ordering of existing gates than a gap; flagged uncertain.

response.plan_implied_asker: a systematic/quant alt-data signals desk with ML engineering capacity and a diversified multi-name book, not a concentrated fundamental shop
response.what_would_falsify: Gate fails (and the plan stops, no fallback) if beta-hat is not positive and significant under the company-block bootstrap, falls outside [0.5,1.5], within-company partial correlation is below 0.45 or negative for a third of firms, or leave-one-out moves beta-hat >30% / flips significance. Conditional on a gate pass, the nowcast is 'not demonstrated' unless it beats damped persistence by >=15% RMSE, Clark-West p<0.05, and >60% directional accuracy on growth-rate change.

issues.summary: The nowcast stage (pooled fixed-effects ridge tuned by nested CV, empirical-Bayes shrinkage weighted by variance ratios) is production ML infrastructure, which the firm explicitly will not build, and it cannot be defended point-by-point to a PM the way the gate regression can.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The brief states this firm has a 3-person data team and one engineer, buys panel data, and 'will not build production ML.' A ridge model with a nested cross-validation loop and hyperparameter selection is exactly that category, distinct from the panel/cohort work the firm is described as routinely capable of.
issues.what_breaks: After the gate passes, the deliverable that actually drives position sizing (the nowcast) is a model this team cannot maintain or re-estimate reliably each quarter, and a PM cannot interrogate the ridge penalty or shrinkage weights the way they can interrogate a fixed-effects beta.
issues.fix: Use the gate-stage fixed-effects coefficient itself as the nowcast (a simple pooled-with-FE point estimate, or basic partial pooling toward the pooled mean weighted by inverse variance computed by hand), and drop ridge/nested CV unless the simple version is shown to fail on the walk-forward test.

issues.summary: The plan escalates to ridge plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage without first showing that the simpler company-FE regression already estimated in the gate stage is inadequate as a forecast.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate regression already produces a per-company beta and pooled beta; the walk-forward validation section could be run on that estimate directly before adding a second, more opaque model layer, but the plan moves straight to the ridge/shrinkage version.
issues.what_breaks: Extra researcher degrees of freedom (ridge penalty choice, shrinkage weighting) are introduced before the plan has shown they are needed, making the eventual RMSE improvement harder to attribute and harder to defend as not being tuned to the test set despite the embargo.
issues.fix: Run the walk-forward validation on the plain FE estimate first; only add ridge/shrinkage if that baseline demonstrably underperforms damped persistence by a margin the simple version cannot close.

issues.summary: Multiple commercial panel vendors (Similarweb, Comscore, M Science, Yipit-style, Sensor Tower, data.ai) appear to be licensed as part of the standard data build rather than added only after the gate on a primary vendor and a small seed sample (ADP, Paycom, Paylocity, Dayforce) has passed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate is explicitly the kill point ('gate failure yields a negative result... not a fallback'), and the seed sample of clean seat-disclosers is small enough to test cheaply with one panel vendor; committing to a multi-vendor replication panel before that gate is decided spends licensing budget the kill criterion is designed to make unnecessary if it fails.
issues.what_breaks: If the gate fails on the cheap subsample, the replication and mobile panel licenses are sunk cost with no further use, which is exactly the spend-before-cheap-test pattern the review is meant to catch.
issues.fix: Run the gate on the primary vendor against the 4-6 cleanest seat-disclosers first; only license replication and mobile panels once that gate passes.

issues.summary: Web-traffic and app-usage panels on public SaaS names are widely subscribed commercial products, and the plan never addresses why a MAU-to-ARR nowcast built on the same vendors other funds already buy would still be mispriced.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Similarweb and Sensor Tower data on names like Dropbox, Atlassian, Asana and monday.com is standard alt-data fare in long/short SaaS coverage; the plan's consensus-surprise regression is a good empirical check but the write-up never states what current consensus assumes about this MAU-ARR link or why it would be wrong, leaving the edge case implicit rather than argued.
issues.what_breaks: If the relationship is already reflected in sell-side estimates via the same data, the surprise-regression test will correctly show no edge, but the plan will have spent the full data and modeling budget before learning that, since crowding was never assessed up front.
issues.fix: Before building the nowcast, check how many of the target companies already have sell-side or buy-side notes referencing app/web traffic data, and treat that as a cheap prior on how much of the surprise regression's power is already used up.

response.overall: The gate-and-nowcast structure is well-designed for its stated goal: it front-loads a real kill test, decomposes ARR growth into seat and price components before modeling, states explicit falsification thresholds, and works through the mechanism's failure modes (contracted vs. active seats, free tiers, enterprise blindness, disclosure endogeneity) rather than just listing generic pitfalls. The core defect is a mismatch between the sophistication of the nowcast stage and what this firm can build, maintain, and defend to a PM oss-validated ridge with empirical-Bayes shrinkage is production ML the firm explicitly rejected, and it sits on top of a fixed-effects regression that may already be a sufficient, far more explainable forecast. Trim the nowcast to the simple estimate, defer multi-vendor spend until the gate passes, and this becomes a plan the stated firm can actually run and stand behind.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. The firm-fit reading is arguable — a pooled ridge with nested CV and empirical-Bayes shrinkage is a standard research-side estimator, not 'production ML' infrastructure, and a 3-person data team plus engineer can run it in a notebook, so the label is a stretch. But the underlying point that the quarter-over-quarter deliverable driving position sizing becomes a model whose penalty and shrinkage weights a PM cannot interrogate the way they can interrogate a fixed-effects beta is grounded in this brief's explicit 'defensible to a PM who will ask what would have to be true' requirement, and the plan really does put the opaque layer at the decision-relevant stage. Torn, so escalating.

Not in gold, and specific to this plan: the gate stage already estimates a company-FE beta that could itself be walk-forward tested, yet the plan jumps to ridge plus EB shrinkage with no stated condition under which the simpler estimate would have sufficed. That adds tuning degrees of freedom (penalty, shrinkage weighting) ahead of any demonstration they are needed, which cuts against the plan's own pre-registration and specification-count discipline. A desk would take this seriously.

Not in gold and not contradicting the anti-objection — it does not complain that the seat-disclosing sample is thin; it uses that thinness as the reason the gate can be tested cheaply on one primary vendor first. The concern is ordering of spend: the data section commits to a replication panel plus two mobile vendors as part of the standard build, while the plan's own kill criterion makes that spend unnecessary if the gate fails. Legitimate sequencing point about this plan's stated cost structure.

Crowding/no-edge is a canonical alt-data objection and the plan partly pre-empts it: pre-print consensus is an explicit baseline and the surprise-space regression is precisely a test of whether the link is already in estimates — the evaluator concedes both. That makes the bite weaker than presented, and the naming of Similarweb/Sensor Tower on Dropbox/Atlassian/Asana would read similarly against any SaaS web-panel plan. Still, the sharper version — the plan never states what consensus currently assumes about the MAU-to-seat link or why it would be wrong, so crowding is only learned at the end of the budget rather than argued up front — is a real gap in a plan whose output must be defended to a PM. Borderline, escalating.

response.plan_implied_asker: A systematic research/data-science team building a reusable ID-to-institution matching capability, optimizing for statistical robustness of the clustering rather than for the downstream sizing decision.
response.what_would_falsify: If the 100-permutation null (customers reshuffled at fixed institution size) is not beaten at the 99th percentile of silhouette, or cluster-wise bootstrap Jaccard falls below 0.60, or cross-window ARI falls below 0.40, the plan requires reporting the negative: only country and rough business-model separation are supportable, not named-institution identification.

issues.summary: The Hungarian-algorithm identity match — the single step where a wrong call directly causes a mis-sized position — ranks institutions by raw panel customer count against real market share, without applying the panel-composition correction the plan itself prescribes elsewhere.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan explicitly acknowledges the panel skews young/urban/digital/multi-banked and prescribes panel-reweighted shares for the feature aggregates, but the naming step ('rank IDs by panel customers, institutions by market share; Hungarian on rank distance') uses raw customer counts. A fast-growing neobank could easily out-rank a larger incumbent in raw panel presence while remaining smaller by true deposit share — exactly the kind of confidently wrong, high-conviction match the desk is most exposed to, since the margin/rank-agreement gates would pass on a systematically biased input rather than catch it.
issues.what_breaks: Tier B/C naming: a bank could clear the ≤3-candidate, rank-agreement, and margin thresholds while being matched to the wrong ticker, because the underlying panel-share ranking is biased in a known, correctable direction.
issues.fix: Apply the same panel-reweighting used for feature aggregates to the customer-count ranking that feeds the Hungarian assignment (e.g., reweight by known population/segment shares before ranking), and run the naming step both raw and reweighted — flag any institution whose tier or candidate ranking changes between the two as unresolved rather than accepted.

issues.summary: The full feature build (60-80 features, external ECB/EBA/national central bank/SPACE data) and the triple-algorithm clustering ensemble are constructed in full before the cheapest viability check (whether IDs separate at all) is run.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The silhouette/Calinski-Harabasz gate that can kill the whole approach ('<0.25 = no') only fires after the entire feature engineering and multi-source external data ingestion is complete and after Ward/GMM/HDBSCAN have all been run and reconciled — for a 1-engineer team this is substantial sunk setup before the first real signal on whether the premise holds at all.
issues.what_breaks: If IDs turn out not to separate meaningfully, the team has already built the full external-data pipeline and feature set before learning this, rather than after a cheap pilot.
issues.fix: Run a fast first pass on a reduced feature set (e.g., salary detection, balance, ATM intensity — 10-15 features) with a single clustering algorithm on a subsample of institutions to check gross separability before committing to full feature engineering and external data licensing/collection.

issues.summary: The validation stack as specified (three clustering algorithms reconciled via co-association, 500-iteration bootstrap, run independently across four six-month windows, plus a 100-permutation null) is a large compute and engineering commitment for a team of one engineer and three data staff.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The team composition given is a three-person data-cleaning group plus a single engineer; re-featuring and re-clustering 500 times per window, times four windows, times three base algorithms, is a meaningful build-and-runtime burden that isn't scoped against the team's actual bandwidth or the six-to-eighteen-month decision horizon.
issues.what_breaks: Either the full validation matrix slips the timeline past the point where the identification is useful for the horizon in question, or corners get cut on the bootstrap/window replication under time pressure, quietly weakening exactly the stability checks that are supposed to prevent false-positive naming.
issues.fix: Phase the validation: run the full stack on one window first to get a directional read, and only extend to all four windows and the full 500-iteration bootstrap for institutions that clear the first-pass gates and are actually candidates the desk wants to trade.

response.overall: This is an unusually disciplined plan for the stated purpose: it states its null explicitly, pre-commits a permutation test and stability thresholds, tiers its confidence in identity claims to match the concentrated, Type-I-dominated payoff, and pairs sophisticated clustering machinery with checks a PM can actually inspect (hand-read narratives, pre-committed rubric thresholds, explicit negative-result reporting). The one issue serious enough to block sign-off is that the final identity-matching step — the exact place where a confident wrong match does the damage the PM is worried about — ranks institutions by raw panel customer count without applying the panel-bias correction the plan uses everywhere else, which could produce a plausible-looking but systematically wrong match. Fix that, and consider a cheaper first-pass pilot before the full feature/external-data build, and this plan is fit for purpose.

issue_buckets.why: Same concern as blocking#1: the naming/Hungarian step ranks IDs by raw panel customer count against market share, importing the panel skew the plan itself documents, so a wrong high-conviction name can clear the margin and rank-agreement gates.

Not in gold and specific enough to bite: the external market-structure and payments-habits ingestion (ECB SDW, EBA, NCB reports, scheme lists, SPACE) is only needed for the country/archetype/naming rungs, yet the plan sequences the full 60-80 feature build plus tri-algorithm ensemble before the cheap kill gate (silhouette <0.25) fires. For a one-engineer team that is a genuine ordering criticism, not a recited canonical objection.

Team-bandwidth concern is plausible for a three-person data team plus one engineer, and the 500-iteration bootstrap does require re-featuring from customer-level transactions rather than just re-clustering. But the compute framing is weak on this data: clustering 150-400 institutions in 8-14 PCA dimensions three ways is near-trivial, so the 'large compute commitment' claim is partly unearned and the objection edges toward a generic capacity complaint. Torn, so flagged for escalation.

response.plan_implied_asker: A fund with real (if lean) data infrastructure that can license and clean alt-data panels and is willing to spend months proving a matching pipeline is trustworthy before trading on it, treating a confidently wrong ID-to-ticker match as the catastrophic risk rather than latency, breadth, or backtested Sharpe.
response.what_would_falsify: Share of panel deposit volume assigned at ≥95% precision on held-out institutions falls below 40% for a country (declared not identifiable); permuted fingerprints failing to score at chance or phantom IDs failing to abstain (indicating the scoring is fitting noise/leakage rather than real structure); leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out precision gaps that don't hold at the pre-set 0.80/0.25 margin thresholds.

issues.summary: The anchor-data build (national registries, OSM scraping, tariff PDFs, country-specific benefit-calendar joins, 500-respondent surveys) is specified as one undifferentiated requirement across five countries rather than explicitly gated to the stated pilot order (NL first, stop if it fails).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself sets NL as the cheap kill test, but a 3-person data team plus one engineer will burn most of its capacity standing up DE/ES/FR/PL-specific anchors (Kindergeldnummer digits, AOW/toeslagen, CAF, INPS, tariff scraping) if that work isn't explicitly deferred until NL clears the 40% bar — undermining the very front-loaded-kill structure the pilots are meant to provide.
issues.what_breaks: Effort and calibration time gets sunk into countries whose identifiability hasn't been established yet, defeating the purpose of running NL first.
issues.fix: State explicitly that non-NL anchor acquisition and register-building only begins after the NL pilot clears its threshold, so the team's fixed capacity is spent sequentially rather than in parallel.

issues.summary: Validation is cross-sectional (leave-one-institution-out, leave-one-country-out) but there is no leave-future-quarter-out test, even though the crosswalk will be applied prospectively while positions are held for 6-18 months.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Fingerprints here are built from features like growth correlation and fee signature that are explicitly tied to a fast-moving competitive landscape (N26/Revolut/bunq growth, tariff changes) — the exact kind of thing that can drift within a single holding period, and merger/consolidation handling is addressed for the anchor side but not tested for whether the panel-side match itself degrades as a position ages.
issues.what_breaks: A match validated at time of entry could silently decay in confidence over the following two quarters without the pipeline having any test designed to catch that, and the desk would keep sizing on a mapping that's no longer as reliable as its initial acceptance criteria suggested.
issues.fix: Add a rolling/prospective check: for institutions accepted in an early quarter, re-score using only later-quarter data and report whether acceptance (p≥0.80, margin≥0.25) is stable, not just whether the initial cross-sectional holdout passed.

response.overall: This is an unusually disciplined plan for the stated problem: it fixes a falsifiable threshold up front, treats Type I error as the dominant cost via an abstain sink and high-precision gating rather than forcing assignments, keeps anchors out of the feature-building path via registers.yaml, and backs a genuinely necessary sophisticated method (optimal-transport/min-cost-flow assignment) with simple, PM-legible checks (permutation-at-chance, phantom-ID abstention, confusion matrices, risk-coverage curves). The two gaps worth closing are practical rather than conceptual: sequence the country-specific data engineering so it doesn't outrun the NL kill gate, and add a prospective/out-of-time check so a match's reliability is monitored across the holding period, not just validated at the moment of assignment.

issue_buckets.why: Same substance as blocking#1's maintenance-burden component: the multi-country anchor build (five regulators, OSM, tariff schedules, national benefit-numbering joins, surveys) is unaffordable for a three-person data team and one engineer. Reframed as a sequencing fix (defer DE/ES/FR/PL anchors until NL clears the 40% bar) rather than as disproportionality, and it omits the labels-do-not-exist and GDPR-gate-zero strands, but it is recognisably the same concern about the same plan components.

Not in gold and earned on this plan's specifics rather than recited. The plan's holdout units are explicitly institution and country (LOIO, LOCO) with quarter-versioned fingerprints, and several comparators — growth correlation against N26/Revolut/bunq disclosures, fee_signature against published tariff schedules — are tied to a fast-moving landscape; consolidation is handled on the anchor/roster side but nothing tests whether an accepted match's confidence decays over the 6-18 month hold it will be sized on.
